quotes.name: Gloria Liu
quotes.quote: When a new student comes in mid-cycle, the first thing I notice is the quiet. Not the building being quiet, but the way the hallways get a little more careful. Teachers glance up a beat longer when they hear footsteps they don't recognize. The office staff moves a little faster. And the child themselves — they're usually trying to take up as little space as possible, which is the opposite of what we want. Getting them caught up isn't about a test or a worksheet. It's about finding one adult in the building who they trust by the end of the first week. That's the whole job. The academics follow once that trust is there. We're lucky in Rockridge because we have the resources to do that well — small classes, aides who know the kids by name, a PTA that shows up. But I've seen it work in schools with a fraction of our funding, and it always comes down to the same thing: one person who says, 'I've got you.' That's what I look for first, and that's what I make sure happens before we even talk about grade-level standards.

quotes.name: Mei Wong
quotes.quote: In the classroom, a kid can sit still and look like they're following along. In the after-school hours, you see the real picture — who's got energy left, who's running on fumes, who's carrying something from home that has nothing to do with math or reading. When a new kid shows up tired, they don't always say it. They find a corner, they put their head down, or they get a little short with the kids next to them. You learn to read it. You give them a snack and a quiet spot, and you don't push. The classroom has to move forward; we get to wait.

interviews.raw: {"answer":"I see it in the first week, every time. A new student walks in and they're not really listening to me yet — they're reading the room. They're counting the exits, figuring out who sits with who, trying to find the one kid who looks like they might be okay to talk to. The questions they ask are never about the syllabus. It's 'where's the bathroom,' 'is the cafeteria food actually that bad,' 'who's the teacher everyone's scared of.' They're not worried about biology yet. They're worried about belonging. And honestly, that's the real lesson of that first week — not the content, but showing them this is a place where they can land. We've got a strong school here, and I think sometimes people assume that means it's easy for the new kid. It's not. Strong schools still have to prove themselves to a sixteen-year-old who just moved neighborhoods and doesn't know a single face in the hallway. That's the work I actually do in September. The science comes after they feel safe enough to ask a real question.","fact_ids":["F-eec877f19193","F-6ab7a01ec296"],"basis":"lived-context","unverifiedLead":null,"abstain_reason":null}
